title: Canada Expands Low-Wage Foreign Worker Access for Multi-Site Employers Under New TFWP Rules
excerpt: Employers with multiple small work locations can now hire one or two temporary foreign workers per site, broadening access beyond the usual 10% workforce cap.
body:
• Employment and Social Development Canada now allows multi-site employers to hire one or two low-wage temporary foreign workers per location with fewer than 10 employees, up from an earlier nationwide calculation that often yielded zero permits for small sites.
  • The change applies to the Temporary Foreign Worker Program's low-wage stream, where positions pay below 120% of the regional median wage — C$36.92 per hour in Ontario.
  • In-demand sectors such as healthcare, construction and food production can place up to two workers per qualifying site, while other employers are limited to one.
  • Canada plans to admit 60,000 workers through the TFWP and 170,000 through the International Mobility Program this year.

What Changed

Through a quiet update to its program webpage on August 18, 2026, Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) loosened the workforce cap on low-wage temporary foreign workers for employers with multiple small work locations. The adjustment targets a gap that had made it mathematically impossible for some employers to hire even a single foreign worker under the existing formula.

Under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program, employers are generally allowed to fill no more than 10% of their workforce with low-wage foreign workers — or 20% if they operate in healthcare, construction or food production. When a company's total workforce at a given location falls below 10 employees, that percentage calculation can round down to zero.

ESDC's new approach shifts the cap calculation to use the number of employees at each individual work location rather than the national headcount. Employers in standard sectors can now hire one low-wage temporary foreign worker per small location, while those in in-demand sectors can hire two.

How the Cap Works in Practice

The workforce calculation at each location includes all full-time and part-time employees, workers with approved Labour Market Impact Assessments (LMIAs) who have not yet started, and vacant positions listed on pending LMIA applications. Part-time employees — those averaging fewer than 30 hours per week — count as 0.5 of a worker.

A position qualifies as low-wage if it pays below 120% of the regional median wage listed on the federal Job Bank. In Ontario, that threshold currently sits at C$36.92 per hour. Workers hired above this threshold go through the high-wage stream, which is not subject to the workforce cap.

Employers hiring through the low-wage stream must still meet additional obligations: paying for the worker's transportation to and from Canada, ensuring access to housing costing less than 30% of pre-tax income, and purchasing private health insurance for workers not covered by provincial plans.

Broader Context

The update builds on a March 2026 change that empowered provinces to raise the low-wage workforce cap to 15% in rural areas. It also comes against the backdrop of a September 2024 moratorium on LMIAs for low-wage positions in urban areas with unemployment above 6%, which remains in effect.

Canada's 2026 immigration levels plan allocates 60,000 admissions through the TFWP and 170,000 through the International Mobility Program, which does not require an LMIA. The majority of work permits continue to flow through the IMP rather than the more restrictive TFWP pathway.
